COMPTROLLER’S DECISION

This decision is considered final on February 12, 2024, unless a motion for rehearing is timely filed; this date of finality is calculated based on the Administrative Procedure Act (APA).[1] The failure to timely file a motion for rehearing may result in adverse legal consequences.

Administrative Law Judge (ALJ) Keneshia Washington of the State Office of Administrative Hearings (SOAH) issued a Proposal for Decision (PFD) that includes Findings of Fact and Conclusions of Law. SOAH served the PFD on each party and each party was given an opportunity to file exceptions and replies with SOAH in accordance with SOAH’s rules of procedure. The ALJ recommended that the Comptroller adopt the PFD as written.

After review and consideration, IT IS ORDERED that the PFD is adopted as changed.[2]

The result from this Decision is Attachment A. The ALJ’s recommendation letter is Attachment B. The PFD as changed is Attachment C. Attachments A, B, and C are incorporated by reference.

Attachment A reflects a credit owed to Petitioner.

The credit will be processed after the date the comptroller’s decision is final. The parties may waive the right to file a motion for rehearing to expedite the processing of the credit. A waiver of rehearing or motion for rehearing may be filed as described above.

SIGNED on this 17th day of January 2024

GLENN HEGAR

Comptroller of Public Accounts

By: Lisa Craven

Deputy Comptroller

ATTACHMENT C

SOAH Docket No. 304-23-08113

TCPA Hearing No. 115,379

**************

TAXPAYER NO: **************

v.

TEXAS COMPTROLLER OF PUBLIC ACCOUNTS

BEFORE THE STATE OFFICE OF ADMINISTRATIVE HEARINGS

Proposal for Decision

**************(Petitioner) was audited for sales and use tax compliance by the Tax Division (Staff) of the Texas Comptroller of Public Accounts (Comptroller). Petitioner was assessed tax, a 10% penalty for late filed periods, and interest. It requested redetermination, contending eligibility for a myriad of tax exemptions, including sale for resale, water-related exemptions, and manufacturing-related exemptions. Petitioner also contends the audit erroneously assesses nontaxable items, such as services not enumerated in Texas Tax Code § 151.0101. Furthermore, Petitioner contends that it is eligible for credits for tax erroneously paid to vendors erroneously for various reasons, including nontaxable periodic maintenance of real property and payment of tax in excess of the applicable tax rate. Staff agreed to adjustments, but asserts Petitioner failed to prove error in the proposed amended audit. In this Proposal for Decision, the Administrative Law Judge (ALJ) recommends that the assessment against Petitioner be affirmed except as agreed to by Staff.

I. NOTICE, JURISDICTION, AND PROCEDURAL HISTORY

Staff referred the contested case to the State Office of Administrative Hearings (SOAH) and, on December 20, 2022, ALJ Keneshia Washington issued an Order Setting Written Submission Requirements, which set the written submission hearing, filing deadlines, and record closing date of May 1, 2023. On December 28, 2022, Staff issued Petitioner a Notice of Hearing by Written Submission. Petitioner was represented by **************. Daniel Neuhoff represented Staff.

There are no issues of notice or jurisdiction; therefore, those matters are set out in the Findings of Fact and Conclusions of Law without further discussion.

II. REASONS FOR DECISION

A. EVIDENCE PRESENTED

Staff provided the pleadings the parties exchanged prior to referring the matter to SOAH and offered the following exhibits:

1. Hearing Request Receipt;

2. Texas Notification of Audit Results;

3. Penalty & Interest Waiver Worksheet;

4. Audit Report;

5. Audit Plan;

6. Independent Audit Review (IAR) Report; and

7. Contested Refund Items Spreadsheet.

Petitioner offered the following exhibits attached to its pleadings:

1. Detail Vendor Listing;

2. Sales and Use Tax Accrual Breakout Schedule;

3. GL Accrued Sales Tax January 1, 2011 – August 28, 2017; and

4. Summary Sheet of Requested Credits.

B. AGREED ADJUSTMENTS

Staff agreed to adjustments as shown in its Exhibit 7.

C. FACTS ESTABLISHED AND ISSUES PRESENTED

During the period at issue, Petitioner manufactured corn tortillas, flour tortillas, and tortilla chips for sale to distributors, retailers, and restaurants. Petitioner did not sell meals ready to eat. Petitioner operated from a facility in CITY-1, Texas and opened a new manufacturing facility in CITY-2, Texas during the audit period. It purchased new equipment and moved old equipment from the CITY-1 location. Petitioner performed its general and administrative operations from the CITY-2 office.

In August 2014, Staff initiated a sales and use tax compliance audit of Petitioner for the period February 1, 2011, August 1, 2014 through July 31, 2014 Spetember 30, 2017. Petitioner provided the auditor with financial statements, trial balances, a list of current acquisitions, product line codes, general ledgers, federal income tax returns, a chart of accounts, depreciation schedules, purchase invoices, contracts, and job files for review. Petitioner also provided an internal equipment list and excel spreadsheets showing the accrual or non-accrual of tax on equipment for which the vendor did not charge sales and use tax.

Source: See Finding of Fact No. 4.

Staff conducted several plant tours of Petitioner’s facilities. An Independent Audit Review (IAR) conference was held with Petitioner and Staff on November 10, 2015. Auditors conducted an additional plant tour following the conference, and Petitioner provided additional information and documentation by August 25, 2016. The IAR reviewer issued a report on December 15, 2016.

Based on the documentation provided and observations during the plant tours, the auditor removed the following assets and expenses from the schedules: an evaporating cooler, industrial gloves, rollers, repairs and maintenance performed on exempt equipment, and push or pull devices as buttons on exempt equipment that are not hand tools. Petitioner provided documentation showing that the X-ray machine was being used to scan for metal objects in the food and was required by federal law. Therefore, the auditor removed it from the assessment. The auditor agreed the corn was washer was exempt because it changed the product. He deemed some IT infrastructure equipment as exempt as part of the manufacturing process.

Petitioner established that CITY-2 ordinances require wastewater to have a pH of less than 5.5 or more than 11.0 standard units before being introduced into publicly owned treatment works. Petitioner’s purchases of chemicals to achieve that pH were deemed tax exempt and not scheduled as errors in the audit.

Petitioner purchased what it asserted was a blast freezer that was used in the manufacturing process. During the plant tours, auditors observed that Petitioner used it to store finished goods for customer pickup rather than to apply an operational blast to the tortillas or chips. Petitioner purchased the freezer and associated parts without paying tax to the vendor who was not permitted to remit sales and use tax to the Comptroller. The auditor scheduled taxable asset purchases, including the freezer and associated parts and services, in Exams 500 and 550.

During the plant tours, the auditors observed that Petitioner had a conveyor system throughout the plant. Some conveyor belts passed through a cooling room. The conveyers were covered in mesh and had holes to facilitate the passage of air. Cooling conveyer system purchases are scheduled as taxable asset purchases in Exam 510. Expenses regarding the conveyors are scheduled in sample exam 610 and detail Exam 630.

The auditor observed that Petitioner purchased the following taxable items and did not accrue tax or pay tax to the vendor: a wastewater treatment system not used to change the pH of the wastewater, silos to store raw materials, lubricants, oil tanks, equipment down payments, deep floor cleaning, and electrical work on taxable equipment. Moreover, Petitioner purchased maintenance and repair services, and the vendor charged a lump-sum amount without itemizing the equipment that was worked on. The invoices also did not specify if any specific amount of the lump-sum charge was attributable to tax. For many of the purchases for construction in progress, there are no itemized sales tax amounts in the vendor contracts or vendor invoices. Instead, the contracts state “all taxes and fees included in the price.” Therefore, the entire lump sum charges are scheduled. During the plant tours, the auditor observed counters and stackers, pumps used to transport food products, conveyor systems, a cooling room, silos, and a freezing room used to store finished food. Taxable purchases of assets used for construction in progress are scheduled in Exam 550.

The auditor used a sample procedure to review expenses and relied on Petitioner’s general ledger and chart of accounts to determine accounts of interest. An accrual flag on the general ledger indicated the purchases for which Petitioner accrued tax to the Comptroller. Scheduled expenses include towels, latex gloves that are neither disposable nor required by a local health inspector or government agency, and computer equipment. Petitioner purchased chemicals that separate the corn husk from the wastewater by solidifying the corn husk for removal and disposal so that it does not cause an obstruction or blockage in the city’s water system. The auditor deemed these purchases taxable because the chemicals did not make a chemical or physical change to the products for sale and were not required by government mandate.

Purchase invoices demonstrated that Petitioner purchased third-party software consulting and data processing services in the form of moving data back-ups to file servers as well as copying, configuring, and loading Petitioner’s database. The vendor of those services billed the consulting and data processing services as a lump sum. The auditor assessed these services as taxable data processing, applying the 20% exemption. Petitioner also purchased taxable cleaning services for its rental uniforms. Taxable expense purchases based on available invoices, the chart of accounts, and the general ledger are scheduled in sample exams 610 and 620. Petitioner’s expense purchases pursuant to a technical support service agreement are scheduled in detail exam 630.

During the period at issue, Petitioner did not pay sales tax on most of its utilities. Because Petitioner did not have a utility study available for its CITY-2 location, the auditor requested predominant use studies to determine the applicability of the exemption for electricity used to power exempt equipment. Petitioner provided a predominant use study for electricity. The study indicated that electric service meter 1 was not exempt from sales tax and that Petitioner uses electricity to power equipment that is not exempt from tax. Taxable expense purchases for electricity utilities are scheduled in detail Exam 670. The auditor observed that Petitioner performed most of the cooking and processing using natural gas. The auditor scheduled credits for any tax paid on natural gas used in manufacturing in Exam 900.

During the plant tour, the auditor observed that on the corn manufacturing line that corn tortillas were counted and stacked and then forwarded down a conveyor to a “Tortilla Cutter” or “Chip Chopper” to cut corn tortillas into chips. Staff agreed that the tortilla cutters were used in the processing including in Petitioner’s manufacturing activities. The plant foreman informed the auditor that the Chip Choppers could be added to the corn manufacturing line or removed at any time for all the corn manufacturing lines on the plant floor depending on whether the customer purchased chips or tortillas. On the flour manufacturing line, the tortillas were counted, stacked, and then forwarded down a conveyor to a wrapping and packaging machine.

The auditor scheduled credits for the Auto Stack Indexes and Counter Stackers when the tortillas transferred directly from the machines to the wrapping and packaging equipment without any interim processing, namely cutting. The auditor did not allow a wrapping and packaging exemption if further processing was performed. The auditor observed three Auto Stack Indexes and Counter Stackers that went directly to wrapping and packaging equipment. The auditor allowed credits for these three items and services performed on them.

Petitioner requested credit for sales tax on the installation of 9,000 feet of 6-inch gas line. However, there is no evidence of sales tax collected in error by the vendor because the amount of the lump-sum price attributable to tax is not clear. The auditor denied the request.

Petitioner requested credit for sales tax paid to its vendor for the installation of corn and flour silos and related equipment. Some silos were constructed outside of Petitioner’s existing building, so the auditor considered the foundations for them as new construction and scheduled credits in Exam 910. However, some of the services purchased from the same vendor did not involve the construction of silos but were for the assembly of a pneumatic conveying system. Credits were denied for those purchases because they constituted taxable assembly of tangible personal property.

Petitioner also requested credits for purchases related to the construction of new foundations for its freezers. Based on the plant tours and available documentation, the auditor deemed the work to be taxable real property remodeling rather than new construction because the result of the work was a thicker floor within an existing structure to accommodate the freezer instead of the creation of new useable square footage. Petitioner’s request for the credits was denied.

Petitioner also requested credits for tax paid to its vendor on the construction of 12-foot-deep concrete wastewater pits created for holding wastewater. Because new, usable space was created, the auditor allowed the credits as scheduled in Exam 910. The auditor observed that a corn cooking boiler was involved in Petitioner’s manufacturing process, so he scheduled credits for tax paid on the purchase in Exam 910. He also scheduled credits for new construction work regarding a new road, a transformer foundation, a dumpster pad, and paving at a dock door in Exam 910 based on documentation provided.

On April 12, 2017, Staff issued a Texas Notification of Audit Results to Petitioner. The assessment included tax, 10% penalty for late filed periods, and interest. Petitioner timely requested redetermination. During the redetermination process, Petitioner provided additional information and documentation, and Staff agreed to adjustments shown in its Exhibit 7. However, disputes remain, and Staff referred the matter to SOAH.

D. ALJ’S ANALYSIS AND RECOMMENDATION

The law requires retailers to keep records that reflect the total gross receipts from sales and the total purchases of taxable items. Tex. Tax Code § 151.025; 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 3.281(b). At a hearing, a taxpayer must produce contemporaneous records and supporting documentation for the transactions in question to substantiate and enable verification of the taxpayer’s claim related to the amount of tax, penalty, or interest to be assessed, collected, or refunded. 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 1.26(a); Tex. Tax Code § 111.0041.

1. Manufacturing

Texas imposes a tax on each sale of a taxable item in this state. Tex. Tax Code § 151.051. The term “taxable item” includes tangible personal property and taxable services. Id. § 151.010. When tax is imposed on tangible personal property the taxing entity’s prima facie burden of proof is easily met because, unless an exemption applies, all sales of tangible personal property in this state are taxable. See, e.g., Comptroller’s Decision No. 116,506 (2020).

A taxpayer has the burden to prove by clear and convincing evidence that the taxpayer or a transaction qualifies for an exemption. 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 1.26(c). Clear and convincing evidence demonstrates the thing to be proved is highly probable. See Black’s Law Dictionary (11th ed. 2019); see also Comptroller’s Decision No. 101,773 (2011). Statutory exemptions are strictly construed and all doubts concerning exemption claims are resolved in favor of the taxing authority. See North Alamo Water Supply Corp. v. Willacy County Appraisal Dist., 804 S.W.2d 894, 899 (Tex. 1991); Sharp v. Tyler Pipe Indus. Inc., 919 S.W.2d 157, 161 (Tex. App.—Austin 1996, writ denied); Sharp v. Chevron Chem. Co., 924 S.W.2d 429, 432 (Tex. App.—Austin 1996, writ denied).

Tangible personal property that will be sold, leased, or rented to, or stored, used, or consumed by a manufacturer is exempt from sales and use tax if the tangible personal property is directly used or consumed in or during the actual manufacturing, processing, or fabrication of tangible personal property for ultimate sale and the use or consumption of the property is necessary or essential to the manufacturing, processing, or fabrication operation and directly makes or causes a chemical or physical change to the product being manufactured, processed, or fabricated for ultimate sale. Tex. Tax Code § 151.318(a)(2)(A). Manufacturing includes each operation beginning with the first stage in the production of tangible personal property and ending with the completion of tangible personal property having the physical properties including packaging, if any, that it has when transferred by the manufacturer to another. Id. § 151.318(d).

The manufacturing exemption includes tangible personal property used or consumed in the actual manufacturing, processing, or fabrication of tangible personal property for ultimate sale if the use or consumption of the property is necessary and essential to a pollution control process, a quality control process that tests tangible personal property that is being manufactured, processed, or fabricated for ultimate sale, or to comply with federal, state, or local laws or rules that establish requirements related to public health. Id. § 151.318(a)(5), (8), (10). The exemption includes safety apparel or work clothing that is used during the actual manufacturing, processing, or fabrication of tangible personal property for ultimate sale if the manufacturing process would not be possible without the use of the apparel or clothing and the apparel or clothing is not resold to the employee. Id. § 151.318(a)(9). The exemption also includes tangible personal property specifically installed to reduce water use and wastewater flow volumes from the manufacturing, processing, fabrication, or repair operation; reuse and recycle wastewater streams generated within the manufacturing, processing, fabrication, or repair operation; or treat wastewater from another industrial or municipal source for the purpose of replacing existing freshwater sources in the manufacturing, processing, fabrication, or repair operation. Id. § 151.318(a)(11).

The manufacturing exemption does not include intraplant transportation equipment, including intraplant transportation equipment used to move a product or raw material in connection with the manufacturing process and specifically including all piping and conveyor systems. Tex. Tax Code § 151.318(c)(1). Intraplant transportation equipment is taxable even if manufacturing or processing activities (such as cooling, mixing, or pollution containment) occur during the transportation of product or component parts of the product. 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 3.300(c)(5).

However, the manufacturing exemption includes piping or conveyor systems that are a component part of a single item of manufacturing equipment or pollution control equipment eligible for the exemption under Subsection (a)(2), (a)(4), or (a)(5). Tex. Tax Code § 151.318(c)(1)(A). Also included are piping through which the product or an intermediate or preliminary product that will become an ingredient or component part of the product is recycled or circulated in a loop between the single item of manufacturing equipment and the ancillary equipment that supports only that single item of manufacturing equipment if the single item of manufacturing equipment and the ancillary equipment operate together to perform a specific step in the manufacturing process. Id. § 151.318(c)(1)(B). Furthermore, the exemption includes piping through which the product or an intermediate or preliminary product that will become an ingredient or component part of the product is recycled back to another single item of manufacturing equipment and its ancillary equipment in the same manufacturing process. Id. § 151.318(c)(1)(C).

For purposes of Texas Tax Code Section 151.318(c)(1), piping through which material is transported forward from one single item of manufacturing equipment and its ancillary support equipment to another single item of manufacturing equipment and its ancillary support equipment is not considered a component part of a single item of manufacturing equipment and is not exempt. Id. § 151.318(f). An integrated group of manufacturing and processing machines and ancillary equipment that operate together to create or produce the product or an intermediate or preliminary product that will become an ingredient or component part of the product is not a single item of manufacturing equipment. Id.

Hand tools and machinery and equipment or supplies used to maintain or store tangible personal property, to the extent not otherwise exempted, are also excluded from the manufacturing exemption. Tex. Tax Code § 151.318(c)(2), (4). A taxpayer claiming a manufacturing exemption has the burden of proof that the exemption is applicable and that no exclusion under Subsection (c) applies. Id. § 151.318(r).

In addition to tangible personal property used in manufacturing, a service that is performed on tangible personal property that, if sold, leased, or rented, at the time of the performance of the service, would be exempted under this chapter because of the nature of the property, its use, or a combination of its nature and use, is exempted from sales and use tax. Id. § 151.3111(a).

As described above, the auditor removed many items from the audit because the items were used in Petitioner’s manufacturing process. The auditor also agreed to credits for tax paid erroneously for manufacturing equipment and services performed on those items. Petitioner contends that additional items are eligible for the manufacturing exemption,

a) Conveyor Belts

The auditor assessed tax on the conveyor belts because they are excluded from the manufacturing exemption as intraplant transportation equipment. Petitioner contends that the conveyors are included in the exemption as conveyor systems that are a component part of a single item of manufacturing equipment. Alternatively, Petitioner contends that the conveyers are directly involved in the processing of products for sale because the holes in the conveyors and the passage through the cold room facilitate completion of the moisture balancing process for the products to arrive at a saleable condition. The cooling also prepares the products for wrapping. However, based on the multiple plant tours and information provided by Petitioner’s foreman, the conveyors transfer the tortillas from one single item of manufacturing equipment to another and are part of an integrated group of manufacturing and processing machines that operate together to produce the products for sale. Tex. Tax Code § 151.318(c)(1); 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 3.300(c)(5).

b) Auto Stack Indexes and Counter Stackers

Petitioner contends that Auto Stack Indexes and Counter Stackers in the corn tortilla and chips manufacturing lines are exempt as involved in wrapping and packaging as the last step in the manufacturing process so that services performed on the equipment are also exempt from tax. However, the machines do not make a chemical or physical change to the products for sale, so each specific machine is not eligible for the manufacturing exemption. When the products are moved from the stackers and counters on conveyor belts to cutters prior to the wrapping and packaging machines, the stackers and counters are removed from the wrapping and packaging process and are not eligible for an exemption from tax. Consequently, services performed on the stackers and counters remain taxable as repair and remodeling of tangible personal property under Texas Tax Code Section 151.0101(a)(5).

c) Rented Uniforms

Petitioner also contends that uniforms and the cleaning services applied to them are eligible for the manufacturing exemption. However, Petitioner has not provided evidence that the uniforms are safety apparel or work clothing that is used during the actual processing of the tortillas, that the manufacturing process would not be possible without the use of the apparel or clothing, and the apparel or clothing is not resold to the employee. Moreover, Petitioner asserts that its freezers are used in the manufacturing process; however, the use of the freezers for storage prior to customer pickup excludes the freezers from the manufacturing exemption. Petitioner has not met its evidentiary burden to establish by clear and convincing evidence that any of the remaining assessed items are eligible for the manufacturing exemption as described above.

2. Other Tax Exemptions

Petitioner contends that scheduled transactions are eligible for other exemptions from tax. It claims that some items are exempt as sales for resale. Because Petitioner does not make taxable sales, this exemption is not applicable. Petitioner also claims that some items are exempt as items taxed by other laws but has not identified under which laws the items are taxed. Petitioner contends that the audit includes tax exempt health care supplies but has not provided documentation to establish that any of the remining assessed items are health care supplies. Moreover, Petitioner contends that scheduled electricity purchases are exempt under Texas Tax Code Section 151.317 but has not provided documentation to establish that any of the remaining assessed expense purchases of electricity are eligible for the exemption. Petitioner contends that it erroneously paid tax on returnable containers but has not provided documentation to establish that any of the scheduled transactions assess tax on returnable containers that are eligible for an exemption. Petitioner has not established by clear and convincing evidence that any tax exemptions apply to the remaining assessed transactions.

3. Services

The Legislature has elected to tax only those services that are specifically enumerated in Texas Tax Code § 151.0101. Thus, the Comptroller has long held that, to impose tax on a service, Staff must demonstrate, prima facie, not only that a service was sold but that the service is taxable. See, e.g., Comptroller’s Decision No. 111,530 (2015).

a) New Construction

In a contested case hearing where the taxability of a service is at issue and the taxpayer raises an exclusionary issue, such as new construction, Staff’s prima facie case must demonstrate not only that the services in question are taxable but also that they are not the type of service excluded from sales and use tax. Comptroller’s Decision No. 117,129 (2022). If Staff demonstrates, prima facie, that a service is taxable and that an exclusion does not apply, it becomes the taxpayer’s burden to prove, by a preponderance of the evidence, that the service is not taxable, or by clear and convincing evidence that the taxable service was exempt from taxation. 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 1.26. A prima facie case is one that allows a fact finder to infer the fact at issue and rule in the party’s favor. See Black’s Law Dictionary (11th ed. 2019); see also Comptroller’s Decision No. 104,533 (2012). A preponderance of the evidence is the greater weight of the evidence, or evidence that is sufficient to incline a fair and impartial mind to one side of any issue rather than the other. See Black’s Law Dictionary (11th ed. 2019).

The repair, remodeling, maintenance, and restoration of tangible personal property, real property services, and real property repair and remodeling are taxable services. Tex. Tax Code § 151.0101(a)(5), (11), (13)(12). New construction is all new improvements to real property; remodeling is rebuilding, replacing, modifying, or upgrading existing real property; and repair is mending or bringing back real property that was broken, damaged, or defective. See 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 3.357(a)(8), (11), (12). A contract that involves both nonresidential remodeling and new construction is taxable in total unless the new construction labor charge is separately stated. Id. § 3.357(b)(3). Documentation that clearly defines the work being performed must be retained to show the new construction and remodeling delineations. Id. §3.357(b)(7). Examples of acceptable documentation are written contracts that detail the scope of work, bid sheets, tally sheets, schedules of values, and blueprints. Id. If there is no written contract for the work, then the service provider should provide a written certification verifying any allocation of charges. Id.

A contractor is any person who builds new improvements to residential or nonresidential real property; completes any part of an uncompleted structure that is an improvement to residential or nonresidential real property; makes improvements to real property as part of periodic and scheduled maintenance of nonresidential real property; or repairs, restores, maintains, or remodels residential real property; and who, in making the improvement, incorporates tangible personal property into the real property that is improved. 34 Tex. Administrative Code §§ 3.357(a)(2), 3.291(a)(3). The contractor shall not collect from a customer any amount represented to be tax on a lump-sum charge or on any portion of the charge. Id. § 3.291(b)(3)(A).

The audit includes assessments for taxable repair and remodeling of tangible personal property, real property services, and real property repair and remodeling services based on documentation provided and the plant tours. Therefore, Staff has met its evidentiary burden of establishing that the scheduled purchases of services are taxable. Moreover, credits for tax erroneously paid on new construction services and nontaxable services are scheduled in the audit as described above. Staff agreed to additional adjustments as shown in its Exhibit 7. Petitioner contends that it is due additional credits and adjustments to the audit based on its purchases of new construction services. Petitioner also asserts that the audit contains nontaxable services and erroneously excludes credits for tax that it paid to vendors for nontaxable services. However, Petitioner has not provided any contracts, scope of work documents, or other evidence to show that it is due additional credits or adjustments for new construction or nontaxable services.

b) Data Processing

Data processing is a taxable service. Tex. Tax Code §§ 151.0035, .0101(a)(12). Twenty percent of the total amount charged for data processing services is exempted from tax. Tex. Tax Code § 151.351; 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 3.330(b). The auditor applied a twenty percent exemption to scheduled data processing services. Petitioner contends that it is due credits for paying 100% of the tax for data processing to its vendors but has not provided documentation to support its contention.

Petitioner contends that the audit is erroneous because it includes assessments of tax paid to its vendors and excludes credits due for tax that it overpaid to its vendors in excess of the applicable tax rate. However, Petitioner has not provided sufficient documentation to show audit error. Because Petitioner has not provided sufficient documentation to meet its evidentiary burdens, the ALJ recommends that the audit be upheld except as agreed to by Staff.

4. Statute of Limitations

Staff asserts the affirmative defense that certain credit requests and contentions were presented outside of statute. Staff references additional credits that Petitioner requested with its amended statement of grounds; however, neither party has identified the purchases at issue. Hence, record evidence does not establish the specific transactions at issue and when those transactions occurred, facts necessary to determining whether the statute of limitations bars the claims. Finally, the issue of whether any of the requested credits is barred by the statute of limitations is moot given that, as described above, Petitioner has not provided sufficient documentation to support additional credits or adjustments to the assessment.

III. FINDINGS OF FACT

1. During the period at issue, ************** (Petitioner) manufactured corn tortillas, flour tortillas, and chips for sale to distributors, retailers, and restaurants.

2. Petitioner did not sell meals ready to eat.

3. Petitioner operated from a facility in CITY-1 and then opened a new manufacturing facility in CITY-2, Texas during the audit period. It purchased new equipment and moved old equipment from the CITY-1 location. Petitioner performed its general and administrative operations from the CITY-2 office.

4. In August 2014, the Tax Division (Staff) of the Texas Comptroller of Public Accounts (Comptroller) initiated a sales and use tax compliance audit of Petitioner for the period February 1, 2011, August 1, 2014 through July 31, 2014 September 30, 2017.

Source: See Staff’s Exhibit No. 2 (Texas Notification of Audit Results) and Exhibit No. 5 (Audit Plan).

5. Petitioner provided the auditor with financial statements, trial balances, a list of current acquisitions, product line codes, general ledgers, federal income tax returns, a chart of accounts, depreciation schedules, purchase invoices, contracts, and job files for review. Petitioner also provided an internal equipment list and excel spreadsheets showing the accrual or non-accrual of tax on equipment for which the vendor did not charge sales and use tax.

6. Staff conducted several plant tours of Petitioner’s facilities. An Independent Audit Review (IAR) conference was held with Petitioner and Staff on November 10, 2015.

7. Auditors conducted an additional plant tour, and Petitioner provided additional information and documentation by August 25, 2016.

8. The IAR reviewer issued a report on December 15, 2016.

9. The auditor removed the following assets and expenses from the schedules: an evaporating cooler, industrial gloves, rollers, repairs and maintenance performed on exempt equipment, and push or pull devices as buttons on exempt equipment that are not hand tools.

10. Petitioner provided documentation showing that the X-ray machine was being used to scan for metal objects in the food and was required by federal law. The auditor removed it from the assessment. He deemed the corn washer exempt because it changed the product. He deemed some IT infrastructure equipment as exempt as part of the manufacturing process.

11. Petitioner established that CITY-2 ordinances require wastewater to have a pH of less than 5.5 or more than 11.0 standard units before being introduced into publicly owned treatment works. Petitioner’s purchases of chemicals to achieve that pH were deemed tax exempt and not scheduled as errors in the audit.

12. During the plant tours, auditors observed that Petitioner used its freezers to store finished goods for customer pickup rather than to apply an operational blast to the tortillas or chips. Petitioner purchased the freezer and associated parts without paying tax to the vendor who was not permitted to remit sales and use tax to the Comptroller. The auditor scheduled taxable asset purchases, including the freezers and associated parts and services, in Exams 500 and 550.

13. During the plant tours, the auditors observed that Petitioner had a conveyor system throughout the plant. Some conveyor belts passed through a cooling room. The conveyers were covered in mesh and had holes to facilitate the passage of air. Cooling conveyer system purchases are scheduled as taxable asset purchases in Exam 510. Expenses regarding the conveyors are scheduled in sample exam 610 and detail Exam 630.

14. The auditor observed that Petitioner purchased the following taxable items and did not accrue tax or pay tax to the vendor: a wastewater treatment system not used to change the pH of the wastewater, silos to store raw materials, lubricants, oil tanks, equipment down payments, deep floor cleaning, and electrical work on taxable equipment.

15. Petitioner purchased maintenance and repair services, and the vendor charged lump sum without itemizing the equipment worked on. The invoices did not specify if any specific amount of the lump-sum charge was attributable to tax. For many of the purchases for construction in progress, there are no itemized sales tax amounts in the vendor contracts or vendor invoices. The contracts state “all taxes and fees included in the price.” Therefore, the entire lump sum charges are scheduled.

16. During the plant tours, the auditor observed counters and stackers, pumps used to transport food products, conveyor systems, a cooling room, silos, and a freezing room used to store finished food. Taxable purchases of assets used for construction in progress are scheduled in Exam 550.

17. The auditor used a sample procedure to review expenses based on the general ledger and chart of accounts. Scheduled expenses include towels, latex gloves that are neither disposable nor required by a local health inspector or government agency, and computer equipment.

18. Petitioner purchased chemicals that separate the corn husk from the wastewater by solidifying the corn husk for removal and disposal so that it does not cause an obstruction or blockage in the city’s water system. The auditor deemed these purchases taxable because the chemicals did not make a chemical or physical change to the products for sale and were not required by government mandate.

19. Purchase invoices showed that Petitioner’s vendor provided third-party software consulting and data processing services in the form of moving data back-ups to file servers as well as copying, configuring, and loading Petitioner’s database. The vendor billed the consulting and data processing services as a lump sum. The auditor applied a twenty percent data processing exemption.

20. Petitioner purchased taxable cleaning services for its rental uniforms.

21. Taxable expense purchases based on available invoices, the chart of accounts, and the general ledger are scheduled in sample exams 610 and 620. Petitioner’s expense purchases pursuant to a technical support service agreement are scheduled in detail exam 630.

22. During the period at issue, Petitioner did not pay sales tax on most of its utilities. Because Petitioner did not have a utility study available for its CITY-2 location, the auditor requested predominant use studies. Petitioner provided a predominant use study for electricity. The study indicated that electric service meter 1 was not exempt from sales tax and that Petitioner uses electricity to power equipment that is not exempt from tax. Taxable expense purchases for electricity utilities are scheduled in detail Exam 670.

23. The auditor observed that Petitioner performed most of the cooking and processing using natural gas. The auditor scheduled credits for any tax paid on natural gas used in manufacturing in Exam 900.

24. During the plant tour, the auditor observed that on the corn manufacturing line that corn tortillas were counted and stacked and then forwarded down a conveyor to a “Tortilla Cutter” or “Chip Chopper” to cut corn tortillas into chips. Staff agreed that the cutters performed processing as part of Petitioner’s manufacturing activities.

25. The plant foreman informed the auditor that the Chip Choppers could be added to the corn manufacturing line or removed at any time for all the corn manufacturing lines on the plant floor depending on whether the customer purchased chips or tortillas.

26. On the flour manufacturing line, the tortillas were counted, stacked, and then forwarded down a conveyor to a wrapping and packaging machine.

27. The auditor scheduled credits for the Auto Stack Indexes and Counter Stackers when the tortillas transferred directly from the machines to the wrapping and packaging equipment without any interim processing, namely cutting.

28. The auditor did not allow a wrapping and packaging exemption if further processing was performed.

29. The auditor observed three Auto Stack Indexes and Counter Stackers that went directly to wrapping and packaging equipment. The auditor allowed credits for these three items and services performed on them.

30. Petitioner requested credit for sales tax on the installation of 9,000 feet of 6- inch gas line. There is no evidence of sales tax collected in error by the vendor because the amount of the lump-sum price attributable to tax is not clear. The auditor denied the request.

31. Petitioner requested credit for sales tax paid to its vendor for the installation of corn and flour silos and related equipment. Some silos were constructed outside of Petitioner’s existing building, so the auditor considered the foundations for them as new construction and scheduled credits in Exam 910.

32. Some of the services purchased from the same vendor did not involve the construction of silos but were for the assembly of a pneumatic conveying system. Credits were denied for those purchases because they constituted taxable assembly of tangible personal property.

33. Petitioner requested credits for construction purchases of new foundations for its freezers. Based on the plant tours and available documentation, the auditor deemed the work to be taxable real property remodeling rather than new construction because the result of the work was a thicker floor within an existing structure to accommodate the freezer instead of the creation of new useable square footage. Petitioner’s request for the credits was denied.

34. Petitioner requested credits for tax paid to its vendor on the construction of 12-foot-deep concrete wastewater pits created for holding wastewater. Because new, usable space was created, the auditor allowed the credits as scheduled in Exam 910.

35. The auditor observed that a corn cooking boiler was involved in Petitioner’s manufacturing process, so he scheduled credits for tax paid on the purchase in Exam 910.

36. The auditor scheduled credits for new construction work regarding a new road, a transformer foundation, a dumpster pad, and paving at a dock door in Exam 910 based on documentation provided.

37. On April 12, 2017, Staff issued a Texas Notification of Audit Results to Petitioner. The assessment included tax, 10% penalty for late filed periods, and interest.

28. Petitioner timely requested redetermination.

39. During the redetermination process, Petitioner provided additional information and documentation.

40. Staff agreed to adjustments shown in its Exhibit 7.

41. Staff referred the contested case to the State Office of Administrative Hearings (SOAH).

42. On December 20, 2022, ALJ Keneshia Washington issued an Order Setting Written Submission Requirements, which set the written submission hearing, filing deadlines, and record closing date.

43. On December 28, 2022, Staff issued Petitioner a Notice of Hearing by Written Submission. The notice contained a statement of the nature of the hearing; a statement of the legal authority and jurisdiction under which the hearing was to be held; a reference to the particular sections of the statutes and rules involved; and a short, plain statement of the factual matters asserted, or an attachment that incorporated by reference the factual matters asserted in the complaint or petition filed with the state agency.

44. The record closed on May 1, 2023.

IV. CONCLUSIONS OF LAW

1. The Comptroller has jurisdiction over these matters. See Tex. Tax Code ch. 111.

2. SOAH has jurisdiction over matters related to the hearing, including the authority to issue a proposal for decision with findings of fact and conclusions of law. See Tex. Gov’t Code ch. 2003.

3. Staff provided a proper and timely notice of hearing. See Tex. Gov’t Code ch. 2001; Tex. Tax Code § 111.009.

4. The law requires retailers to keep records that reflect the total gross receipts from sales and the total purchases of taxable items. Tex. Tax Code § 151.025; 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 3.281(b).

5. At a hearing, a taxpayer must produce contemporaneous records and supporting documentation for the transactions in question to substantiate and enable verification of the taxpayer’s claim related to the amount of tax, penalty, or interest to be assessed, collected, or refunded. 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 1.26(a); Tex. Tax Code § 111.0041.

6. Texas imposes a tax on each sale of a taxable item in this state. Tex. Tax Code § 151.051.

7. The term “taxable item” includes tangible personal property and taxable services. Tex. Tax Code § 151.010.

8. When tax is imposed on tangible personal property the taxing entity’s prima facie burden of proof is easily met because, unless an exemption applies, all sales of tangible personal property in this state are taxable. See, e.g., Comptroller’s Decision No. 116,506 (2020).

9. A taxpayer has the burden to prove by clear and convincing evidence that the taxpayer or a transaction qualifies for an exemption. 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 1.26(c).

10. Clear and convincing evidence demonstrates the thing to be proved is highly probable. See Black’s Law Dictionary (11th ed. 2019); see also Comptroller’s Decision No. 101,773 (2011).

11. Statutory exemptions are strictly construed and all doubts concerning exemption claims are resolved in favor of the taxing authority. See North Alamo Water Supply Corp. v. Willacy County Appraisal Dist., 804 S.W.2d 894, 899 (Tex. 1991); Sharp v. Tyler Pipe Indus. Inc., 919 S.W.2d 157, 161 (Tex. App.—Austin 1996, writ denied); Sharp v. Chevron Chem. Co., 924 S.W.2d 429, 432 (Tex. App.—Austin 1996, writ denied).

12. Tangible personal property that will be sold, leased, or rented to, or stored, used, or consumed by a manufacturer is exempt from sales and use tax if the tangible personal property is directly used or consumed in or during the actual manufacturing, processing, or fabrication of tangible personal property for ultimate sale and the use or consumption of the property is necessary or essential to the manufacturing, processing, or fabrication operation and directly makes or causes a chemical or physical change to the product being manufactured, processed, or fabricated for ultimate sale. Tex. Tax Code § 151.318(a)(2)(A).

13. Manufacturing includes each operation beginning with the first stage in the production of tangible personal property and ending with the completion of tangible personal property having the physical properties including packaging, if any, that it has when transferred by the manufacturer to another. Tex. Tax Code § 151.318(d).

14. The manufacturing exemption includes tangible personal property used or consumed in the actual manufacturing, processing, or fabrication of tangible personal property for ultimate sale if the use or consumption of the property is necessary and essential to a pollution control process, a quality control process that tests tangible personal property that is being manufactured, processed, or fabricated for ultimate sale, or to comply with federal, state, or local laws or rules that establish requirements related to public health. Tex. Tax Code § 151.318(a)(5), (8), (10).

15. The exemption includes safety apparel or work clothing that is used during the actual manufacturing, processing, or fabrication of tangible personal property for ultimate sale if the manufacturing process would not be possible without the use of the apparel or clothing and the apparel or clothing is not resold to the employee. Tex. Tax Code § 151.318(a)(9).

16. The exemption also includes tangible personal property specifically installed to reduce water use and wastewater flow volumes from the manufacturing, processing, fabrication, or repair operation; reuse and recycle wastewater streams generated within the manufacturing, processing, fabrication, or repair operation; or treat wastewater from another industrial or municipal source for the purpose of replacing existing freshwater sources in the manufacturing, processing, fabrication, or repair operation. Tex. Tax Code § 151.318(a)(11).

17. The manufacturing exemption does not include intraplant transportation equipment, including intraplant transportation equipment used to move a product or raw material in connection with the manufacturing process and specifically including all piping and conveyor systems. Tex. Tax Code § 151.318(c)(1).

18. Intraplant transportation equipment is taxable even if manufacturing or processing activities (such as cooling, mixing, or pollution containment) occur during the transportation of product or component parts of the product. 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 3.300(c)(5).

19. The manufacturing exemption includes piping or conveyor systems that are a component part of a single item of manufacturing equipment or pollution control equipment eligible for the exemption under Subsection (a)(2), (a)(4), or (a)(5). Tex. Tax Code § 151.318(c)(1)(A).

20. The manufacturing exemption includes piping through which the product or an intermediate or preliminary product that will become an ingredient or component part of the product is recycled or circulated in a loop between the single item of manufacturing equipment and the ancillary equipment that supports only that single item of manufacturing equipment if the single item of manufacturing equipment and the ancillary equipment operate together to perform a specific step in the manufacturing process. Tex. Tax Code § 151.318(c)(1)(B).

21. The exemption includes piping through which the product or an intermediate or preliminary product that will become an ingredient or component part of the product is recycled back to another single item of manufacturing equipment and its ancillary equipment in the same manufacturing process. Tex. Tax Code § 151.318(c)(1)(C).

22. For purposes of Texas Tax Code Section 151.318(c)(1), piping through which material is transported forward from one single item of manufacturing equipment and its ancillary support equipment to another single item of manufacturing equipment and its ancillary support equipment is not considered a component part of a single item of manufacturing equipment and is not exempt. An integrated group of manufacturing and processing machines and ancillary equipment that operate together to create or produce the product or an intermediate or preliminary product that will become an ingredient or component part of the product is not a single item of manufacturing equipment. Tex. Tax Code § 151.318(f)..

23. Hand tools and machinery and equipment or supplies to the extent not otherwise exempted under this section used to maintain or store tangible personal property are also excluded from the manufacturing exemption. Tex. Tax Code § 151.318(c)(2), (4).

24. A taxpayer claiming an exemption under this section has the burden of proof that the exemption is applicable and that no exclusion under Subsection (c) applies. Tex. Tax Code § 151.318(r).

25. Subject to Section 151.1551, a service that is performed on tangible personal property that, if sold, leased, or rented, at the time of the performance of the service, would be exempted under this chapter because of the nature of the property, its use, or a combination of its nature and use, is exempted from this chapter. Tex. Tax Code § 151.3111(a).

26. Petitioner has not met its evidentiary burden to establish by clear and convincing evidence that any of the remaining assessed items are eligible for the manufacturing exemption.

27. Petitioner has not established by clear and convincing evidence that any tax exemptions apply to the remaining assessed transactions.

28. The Legislature has elected to tax only those services that are specifically enumerated in Texas Tax Code § 151.0101.

29. To impose tax on a service, Staff must demonstrate, prima facie, not only that a service was sold but that the service is taxable. See, e.g., Comptroller’s Decision No. 111,530 (2015).

30. In a contested case hearing where the taxability of a service is at issue and the taxpayer raises an exclusionary issue, such as new construction, Staff’s prima facie case must demonstrate not only that the services in question are taxable but also that they are not the type of service excluded from sales and use tax. Comptroller’s Decision No. 117,129 (2022).

31. If Staff demonstrates, prima facie, that a service is taxable and that an exclusion does not apply, it becomes the taxpayer’s burden to prove, by a preponderance of the evidence, that the service is not taxable, or by clear and convincing evidence that the taxable service was exempt from taxation. 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 1.26.

32. A prima facie case is one that allows a fact finder to infer the fact at issue and rule in the party’s favor. See Black’s Law Dictionary (11th ed. 2019); see also Comptroller’s Decision No. 104,533 (2012).

33. A preponderance of the evidence is the greater weight of the evidence, or evidence that is sufficient to incline a fair and impartial mind to one side of any issue rather than the other. See Black’s Law Dictionary (11th ed. 2019).

34. The repair, remodeling, maintenance, and restoration of tangible personal property, real property services, and real property repair and remodeling are taxable services. Tex. Tax Code § 151.0101(a)(5), (11), (13) (12).

35. New construction is all new improvements to real property; remodeling is rebuilding, replacing, modifying, or upgrading existing real property; and repair is mending or bringing back real property that was broken, damaged, or defective. See 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 3.357(a)(8), (11), (12).

36. A contract that involves both nonresidential remodeling and new construction is taxable in total unless the new construction labor charge is separately stated. 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 3.357(b)(3).

37. Documentation that clearly defines the work being performed must be retained to show the new construction and remodeling delineations. Examples of acceptable documentation are written contracts that detail the scope of work, bid sheets, tally sheets, schedules of values, and blueprints. If there is no written contract for the work, then the service provider should provide a written certification verifying any allocation of charges. 34 Tex. Admin. Code §3.357(b)(7).

38. A contractor is any person who builds new improvements to residential or nonresidential real property; completes any part of an uncompleted structure that is an improvement to residential or nonresidential real property; makes improvements to real property as part of periodic and scheduled maintenance of nonresidential real property; or repairs, restores, maintains, or remodels residential real property; and who, in making the improvement, incorporates tangible personal property into the real property that is improved. 34 Tex. Administrative Code §§ 3.357(a)(2), 3.291(a)(3).

39. The contractor shall not collect from a customer any amount represented to be tax on a lump-sum charge or on any portion of the charge. 34 Tex. Admin Code § 3.291(b)(3)(A).

40. Staff has met its evidentiary burden of establishing that the scheduled purchases of services are taxable.

41. Petitioner has not provided any contracts, scope of work documents, or other evidence to show that it is due additional credits or adjustments for new construction or nontaxable services.

42. Data processing is a taxable service. Tex. Tax Code §§ 151.0035, .0101(a)(12). Twenty percent of the total amount charged for data processing services is exempted from tax. Tex. Tax Code § 151.351; 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 3.330(b).

43. Petitioner has not provided sufficient documentation to show audit error.

44. The audit should be upheld except as agreed to by Staff.
